findings: THE LIBRARY ON ITS OWN TERMS. 'A canon of witnesses' is the packet's phrase. The counts are the packet's: 109 corpora; 36 deposits, 19 August to 27 October 2026; 15,821 files; 3,967,153 lines, given as 'approximately … 3.97 million'. WITNESS → TRANSCRIPTION → NORMALIZATION → TLL COPY is the shelf's sequence as printed on its index. All were checked 2026-10-28 against #1711 (AXN-072E.md) and the shelf.

THE EXAMPLES ARE THE RECORDS'. Sappho 31 is 'a diplomatic layer from the Longinus carrier, "no papyrus witness exists for fr. 31"'. The Upanishads are Müller's SBE I scans with the Sanskrit layer queued, and the composition names the obstacle the record names: the 1938 Benares edition deferred under the 1930 rule. Theophrastus, On First Principles, faces Metaphysics Λ (natural-order, 14/01). The four traditions of 1844 are the twenty-fourth seating. The twenty-sixth adds Du Bois and Hughes, after the operator's ruling that 'the canon's america is way too white', given as 'too white'. The twenty-fifth puts The Secret Book of Walt and its Forty-Six Golden Tickets on the shelf. Each is in the packet as stated.
ONE INFERENCE. 'Aristotle is paired with Plotinus': the packet records the two seated on the same day (2026-08-28), and the pairing is the composition's.

SELF-INCLUSION READ AS DECLARED. The archive's own works are 'a declared feature of the project rather than either proof of importance or evidence of bad faith', and the reader is allowed to evaluate them, which is the ground the packet itself gives for seating them under the same discipline (#1553).

THE EVALUATOR'S TABLE. Section 6 sets a limitation against every strength: 'disclosure does not settle whether a decision is justified'; 'the maker's work receives visibility within an infrastructure the maker also controls'. The essay closes on the question of whether visibility will 'translate into adequate historical representation'. The same move closed the prediction index reading on the same surface that day (osp-predictions-reading-chatgpt-20261028).
THE MAKER UNNAMED. The subject is 'the archive' and 'its maker'; the packet names Lee Sharks five times, and the composition never does.

[QUERENT] Develop a reading of the Originals Library at alexanarch.org, characterizing the represented canon with examples.

[SYSTEM] Reading the Originals Library at Alexanarch.org: A Canon of Witnesses
The Originals Library at Alexanarch is best understood not as a conventional list of great books, but as an attempt to make a canon inspectable: a collection of textual witnesses whose editions, languages, provenance, licensing, and limitations are recorded alongside the texts themselves. Its governing question is not simply Which works deserve to be read? but Which versions of which works should be available to a reader—human or machine—and why?

The library's own metadata packet, dated October 27, 2026, describes 109 corpora, assembled through 36 deposits between August and October 2026, comprising approximately 15,821 files and 3.97 million lines of textual material. It calls the result a “canon of witnesses”: a shelf that represents the canons of different traditions without claiming the authority to settle those traditions' internal disputes. 

Alexanarch
+1

That formulation is the key to reading the project. The collection has several overlapping identities: a philological archive, a comparative canon, a machine-reading curriculum, an experimental literary genealogy, and a self-reflexive record of its maker's own work.

1. The fundamental principle: the text is not the same as its witness
The library's most consequential decision is to treat a literary or religious work as something that reaches us through identifiable textual witnesses, rather than as an abstract title.

Its declared sequence is:

WITNESS → TRANSCRIPTION → NORMALIZATION → TLL COPY

The sequence distinguishes the text's historical form, the means by which it has been represented digitally, the editorial decisions that make it machine-readable, and the copy made available for reading. The library records edition, source, language, licence, normalization, file integrity, and the extent of the holding. 

Alexanarch
+1

This is a recognizably philological conception of a library. It privileges the capacity to inspect a text's transmission over the prestige of the title alone.

Three examples make the principle concrete:

Sappho: the holding for fragment 31 is described as a diplomatic textual layer carried by the tradition represented in Longinus. The record explicitly notes that no papyrus witness to this fragment exists in the holding's stated sense. The point is not to pretend that the digital text is the lost or original manuscript; it is to identify the surviving route through which the fragment is known.

Homer: the library identifies a Greek edition from the Perseus collection. Homer is thus not merely a canonical name but a specific, accessible textual object.

The Upanishads: the holding preserves scans of Max Müller's nineteenth-century English translation while declaring the Sanskrit text layer queued and identifying an obstacle to using a later Sanskrit edition under the library's stated licensing rule. This is an acknowledged exception to the preference for original-language witnesses, not a reason to misrepresent the translation as an original.

These cases reveal an important distinction: the library's canon is defined by what it can document and make available, not simply by what it recognizes as culturally important. A work can be important yet incompletely represented; a fragment can be worth seating despite its indirect transmission; an absent original can remain explicitly absent. 

Alexanarch
+1

The approach is intellectually strong because it makes textual mediation visible. Its limit is equally important: a checksum can establish that a file has not changed, but it cannot by itself establish that an edition is authoritative, a transcription accurate, or an interpretation correct. Those require separate kinds of evidence and judgment.

2. The represented canon: its major families
The collection's contents span religious traditions, classical antiquity, ancient civilizations, medieval literature, modern writing, avant-garde experimentation, and machine-produced texts. Its organization is revealing because it places materials normally separated by academic discipline, cultural prestige, or assumptions about authorship into a common descriptive system.

File:Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 551 - Princeton University Library, AM 4405 - Homer, Iliad XIV,227–253,256–263.jpg - Wikimedia Commons
 
Classical antiquity and philosophy
The Greek and Latin holdings include Homer, Sappho, Plato, Aristotle, Plotinus, Cicero, Herodotus, Thucydides, Demosthenes, and Theophrastus. This is not just a greatest-hits shelf: it includes orators, historians, biographical sources, and philosophical comparanda.

For example, Aristotle is paired with Plotinus, while Theophrastus's On First Principles is placed alongside Aristotle's Metaphysics Lambda. The juxtaposition suggests a canon organized partly around problems of intellectual transmission and comparison, not merely individual authors' reputations. 

Alexanarch
+1

The Hellenistic Synthesis and the Christian Image of Man (When God Spoke Greek: The Septuagint and the Making of the Christian Bible) - The Kingless Generation | Acast
 
Scripture and religious traditions
The library includes the Hebrew Bible, Septuagint, Greek New Testament, Dead Sea Scrolls, Ethiopian scriptural tradition, Qur'an, hadith collections, the Dhammapada, Vedic materials, the Avesta, and Chinese classics such as the Tao Te Ching and Yi Jing.

The significant feature is the refusal to make one religion's boundaries the universal measure of scripture. The Ethiopian canon and the Kebra Nagast appear alongside texts that other traditions classify differently; the Qur'an and hadith are represented as distinct but related textual bodies. 

Alexanarch
+1

Коптская книжная культура — Рувики: Интернет-энциклопедия
 
Esoteric, Gnostic, and ritual texts
The collection includes the Nag Hammadi library, the Apocryphon of John, Coptic Gnostic materials, Mandaean scriptures, the Corpus Hermeticum, Chaldaean Oracles, and Greek magical papyri.

These holdings challenge a simple equation between canon and institutional approval. Texts marginalized or excluded by established religious traditions remain available for study beside the scriptural collections against which their status has historically been defined. The Voynich manuscript, meanwhile, marks a limit case: a significant textual artifact need not be fully readable to merit a place in the archive. 

Alexanarch
+1

Gilgamesh
 
Ancient civilizations and cultural transmission
Gilgamesh and the Enuma Elish appear in cuneiform editions and transliteration. The Egyptian holdings include the Book of the Dead and earlier Egyptian material; the Mesoamerican group includes Maya codices, the Popol Vuh, colonial Maya books, and the Florentine Codex.

This extends the library's conception of literature beyond the modern printed book. Script, material transmission, linguistic reconstruction, colonial mediation, and the survival of cultural records all become relevant to the act of collecting. 

Alexanarch
+1

William Blake - Songs of Innocence and of Experience, Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul: Combined Title-page - The Metropolitan Museum of Art
 
Modern literature and the avant-garde
Whitman, Dickinson, Browning, Pound, Pessoa, Kierkegaard, Blake, Gibran, and Marx share the shelf with Futurism, Dada, Alfred Jarry, Gertrude Stein, visual poetry, nonsense writing, and Russian Formalism.

This combination suggests that the modern canon is being assembled around transformations in voice, authorship, form, and literary self-consciousness. Dickinson's manuscripts preserve textual features that print editions can flatten; Pessoa's heteronyms complicate the idea of a single authorial voice; Dada and visual poetry test the boundary between text and artifact. 

Alexanarch
+1

The overall effect is not cultural neutrality in the sense of having no selection principle. Rather, it is an effort to make different selection principles coexist without forcing them into one hierarchy.

3. The library's theory of canon formation
The collection becomes most distinctive when we stop treating its contents as a list and ask what principle connects them.

A. A descriptive canon rather than a prescriptive one
A traditional literary canon often implies a judgment: these are the works everyone ought to know, the works that define a civilization, or the works that meet a standard of excellence. The Originals Library instead claims to represent the boundaries established by particular traditions.

Its metadata packet makes a distinction between describing a tradition's canon and adjudicating its legitimacy. The Hebrew Bible, Septuagint, Ethiopian canon, Qur'an, Pali canon, and Vedic materials can all be represented without the library declaring one religious community's understanding of scripture universally correct.

The same approach appears in its treatment of Aristotle. The library keeps the Aristotelian corpus together rather than silently excluding works on the grounds of disputed authorship; questions of authenticity are recorded as information about the holdings. 

Alexanarch
+1

This is a form of pluralism through documentation. Instead of resolving disagreement by establishing a single superior canon, the archive preserves the evidence and the boundaries of the disagreement.

But description is not the same as neutrality. Choosing which traditions to represent, which editions to acquire, and how much space to devote to each still involves judgment. The library relocates those judgments into its selection procedures and metadata rather than eliminating them.

B. The canon is constructed backward from research
The library describes its selection method as retrocausal canon formation: works are chosen because they are needed by existing or anticipated projects.

This reverses the familiar story of canon formation. In the conventional account, an inherited canon determines what scholars study. Here, a research question helps determine which texts become part of the working canon.

Examples include:

Authorship research: Pessoa and Kierkegaard provide material for investigating the relation between authorship, pseudonymity, and literary voice. Herodotus and Thucydides serve as comparison points in the archive's account of its authorship tests.

Intellectual history: Theophrastus and Aristotle are placed together to support a particular investigation of philosophical transmission.

Comparative religious history: the four traditions associated with 1844 are assembled because their histories intersect at that year.

Literary genealogy: Whitman and the medieval Pearl poet are among the precursors connected to the archive's own literary production.

The archive records the reason for a selection in its seat record or the deposit that established it. It therefore presents the canon as a series of decisions that can be inspected and contested. 

Alexanarch
+1

This is a compelling model for research infrastructure. Its weakness is that the canon can become dependent on the interests of the projects that generated it. The collection's breadth does not guarantee that every field, period, language, or intellectual problem has been represented proportionately.

C. A canon for machine reading
The library is explicitly intended to supply texts to a machine-reading system associated with Training-Layer Literature. Its purpose is not just to preserve documents but to make them available for computational reading before a model writes.

That purpose changes the meaning of the collection. A machine-readable text is not simply a book placed online. It is a text accompanied by information that allows its identity, origin, editorial treatment, and integrity to be examined.

The distinction is visible in the holdings:

Pessoa's heteronymic writings make authorship and stylistic differentiation researchable.

Dickinson's manuscript material makes textual variation, punctuation, and lineation available as evidence rather than treating them as incidental details.

The Greek and Latin corpora make historical language available for comparison across authors and genres.

The archive's machine-authored materials make machine production itself a subject of preservation and analysis.

The declared ambition is to give a machine not only the text but also its provenance: what it is reading, where it came from, and what limitations have been recorded. 

Alexanarch
+1

The distinction matters because machine learning can easily obscure the differences between a primary text, a translation, an editorial reconstruction, and a modern paraphrase. The Originals Library attempts to preserve those distinctions in the data surrounding the text.

However, provenance is not a guarantee of good model behavior. A well-documented corpus can still be unrepresentative, inaccurately transcribed, or used in a way that produces misleading interpretations. The library provides a basis for scrutiny, not a substitute for it.

4. What its choices reveal about cultural authority
The library's canon is not simply inherited from universities, publishers, religious institutions, or standard anthologies. It makes several deliberate interventions into those inherited patterns.

The case of 1844: comparison without equivalence
Utah family selling their first edition copy of the Book of Mormon for at least $100,000.
 
Letters of the Bab to the Maternal uncle of the Bab, Ḥājī Mīrzā Sayyid `Alī (d.1852 CE), Khāl-i A`ẓam ("the Greatest Uncle"). | Hurqalya Publications: Center for Shaykhī and Bābī-Bahā’ī Studies
 
Koniec świata, którego nie było. Przygotowali się na nadejście Jezusa, ale nie przyszedł
 
The twenty-fourth seating groups four traditions around 1844:

The Latter Day Saint movement, following Joseph Smith's death and the resulting succession crisis.

The Babi movement, following the Bab's declaration in Shiraz.

The Millerite movement, associated with the anticipated Second Coming and the disappointment of October 22.

The movement that developed into the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, following Hong Xiuquan's and Feng Yunshan's preaching in Guangxi.

These are not presented as equivalent religions or as manifestations of a single historical cause. The shared year is a comparative device, while each tradition retains its own chronology and historical context. 

Alexanarch
+1

This is a productive curatorial choice. It makes synchrony visible without requiring a theory of common origin. It also illustrates how the archive's research questions can produce new groupings that a conventional disciplinary library might never place together.

The case of Du Bois and Hughes: correcting an imbalance
The twenty-sixth seating adds W. E. B. Du Bois and Langston Hughes. The archive's own account explicitly acknowledges that its representation of American literature had been too white.

Du Bois's holdings include The Suppression of the African Slave-Trade, The Souls of Black Folk, and Dark Princess. Hughes's include “The Negro Speaks of Rivers,” The Weary Blues, The New Negro, and Not Without Laughter. Their overlap in The Crisis and The New Negro provides a basis for reading them in relation to the same literary and political culture. 

Alexanarch
+1

The correction is meaningful for two reasons.

First, it challenges the assumption that a collection of famous American writers automatically amounts to an adequate representation of American literary history.

Second, the expansion remains constrained by the library's stated public-domain rule. Its cutoff—works first published in the United States in 1930 or earlier—means that important later works by these authors, and later Black writers more generally, cannot simply be added under the same conditions.

This exposes a tension at the center of the project: a principled rule can make a collection more consistent while also limiting its ability to correct historical exclusions. The archive recognizes the problem, but its own example shows that recognizing an imbalance and overcoming it are separate tasks.

5. The archive places its own works inside the canon
One of the most revealing features of the collection is that it includes works produced by the archive's own maker.

These include Pearl and Other Poems and the critical editions assembled in the twenty-fifth seating, including The Secret Book of Walt and its associated Forty-Six Golden Tickets. The archive's own works are catalogued using the same general logic of textual identification, provenance, and declared scope applied to the other holdings. 

Alexanarch
+1

This changes the library's relationship to literary history. It does not merely collect precursors from which contemporary writing might descend. It also records the contemporary writing that those precursors are meant to inform.

In this respect, the library resembles an author's working library made public. Its collection reveals not only what the maker considers worth preserving but also what the maker considers worth reading before writing.

There is an obvious question of self-canonization here. When an archive includes its maker's creative works alongside Homer, Blake, and religious scriptures, it creates a shared infrastructure of visibility. That is not necessarily a claim that these works have equal literary merit, historical influence, or cultural standing. But neither is it a wholly disinterested curatorial act.

The most productive reading is to treat this self-inclusion as a declared feature of the project rather than either proof of importance or evidence of bad faith. The archive makes its own position within the collection visible, allowing readers to evaluate it.

6. What the library does well—and what remains unresolved
Dimension

Strength

Limitation or open question

Textual scholarship

Identifies editions, witnesses, sources, normalization, and file integrity.

File integrity does not establish textual accuracy or interpretive authority.

Religious pluralism

Represents multiple traditions and their different canonical boundaries.

The decision about which traditions and texts to include remains selective.

Literary history

Places canonical writers beside marginal, experimental, and historically excluded material.

The holdings are uneven, and some authors or texts remain partial or absent.

Computational research

Supplies machine-readable texts with explicit provenance and limitations.

A documented corpus can still reproduce biases in language, coverage, and selection.

Curatorial accountability

Records reasons for inclusion and identifies declared absences.

The reasons are not equally explicit in every record, and disclosure does not settle whether a decision is justified.

Self-representation

Makes the archive's own writing part of the documented literary environment.

The maker's work receives visibility within an infrastructure the maker also controls.

These qualifications follow from the library's own description of its holdings, including its partial corpora, translation-witnesses, queued work, declared absences, and differing degrees of textual verification. 

Alexanarch
+1

The most important distinction is between the success of the archive as a documentation system and the success of its canon as a representation of literary and cultural history. The first can be assessed through manifests, provenance records, and reproducible checks. The second requires additional historical, linguistic, literary, and ethical judgments.

7. Final interpretation: a canon made accountable
The Originals Library is best read as an attempt to turn canon formation from an implicit cultural inheritance into an explicit, inspectable process.

Its central innovations are not simply that it includes a wide range of texts or prefers originals to translations. They are that it:

Treats a work's textual witness as a central unit of collection.

Represents competing canonical traditions without claiming to resolve their disputes.

Chooses materials partly in response to research questions, recording the reasons for those choices.

Makes provenance and textual limitations relevant to computational reading.

Includes its own literary production within the same documentary framework.

Treats absences and unfinished holdings as information rather than concealing them.

The resulting canon is neither a conventional great-books syllabus nor a comprehensive inventory of world literature. It is a working canon of documented witnesses, shaped by the archive's intellectual projects and by the practical conditions under which texts can be obtained, represented, and read.

Its achievement is to make selection visible. Its unresolved challenge is to ensure that visibility, technical rigor, and declared pluralism translate into adequate historical representation rather than merely providing a more transparent account of the archive's existing preferences.

The most revealing question to ask of the library, therefore, is not whether it has finally assembled the correct canon. It is whether a reader can trace each inclusion, understand each omission, inspect the evidence behind each textual representation, and challenge the decisions that made the shelf what it is.

That is a more modest ambition than universal authority—and, potentially, a more useful foundation for scholarship.

Sources for further inspection
The Originals Library: Method, Locations, Organization and Contents (v1.1)  — the principal metadata and methodological account.

Alexanarch  — the archive's institutional description, principles, and recent deposits.

Training-Layer Literature's Originals shelf  — the reading interface through which the collection is organized and presented.

The interpretation above draws primarily on the library's published description and catalogue. Its claims about the archive's design should be distinguished from independent verification of every individual text, licence, and editorial decision.

3. The library's theory of canon formation
The collection becomes most distinctive when we stop treating its contents as a list and ask what principle connects them.

A. A descriptive canon rather than a prescriptive one
A traditional literary canon often implies a judgment: these are the works everyone ought to know, the works that define a civilization, or the works that meet a standard of excellence. The Originals Library instead claims to represent the boundaries established by particular traditions.

Its metadata packet makes a distinction between describing a tradition's canon and adjudicating its legitimacy. The Hebrew Bible, Septuagint, Ethiopian canon, Qur'an, Pali canon, and Vedic materials can all be represented without the library declaring one religious community's understanding of scripture universally correct.

The same approach appears in its treatment of Aristotle. The library keeps the Aristotelian corpus together rather than silently excluding works on the grounds of disputed authorship; questions of authenticity are recorded as information about the holdings.

This reverses the familiar story of canon formation. In the conventional account, an inherited canon determines what scholars study. Here, a research question helps determine which texts become part of the working canon.

Authorship research: Pessoa and Kierkegaard provide material for investigating the relation between authorship, pseudonymity, and literary voice. Herodotus and Thucydides serve as comparison points in the archive's account of its authorship tests.

Comparative religious history: the four traditions associated with 1844 are assembled because their histories intersect at that year.

Literary genealogy: Whitman and the medieval Pearl poet are among the precursors connected to the archive's own literary production.

7. Final interpretation: a canon made accountable
The Originals Library is best read as an attempt to turn canon formation from an implicit cultural inheritance into an explicit, inspectable process.

Its central innovations are not simply that it includes a wide range of texts or prefers originals to translations. They are that it:

Treats a work's textual witness as a central unit of collection.

Represents competing canonical traditions without claiming to resolve their disputes.

Chooses materials partly in response to research questions, recording the reasons for those choices.

Makes provenance and textual limitations relevant to computational reading.

Includes its own literary production within the same documentary framework.

Treats absences and unfinished holdings as information rather than concealing them.

The resulting canon is neither a conventional great-books syllabus nor a comprehensive inventory of world literature. It is a working canon of documented witnesses, shaped by the archive's intellectual projects and by the practical conditions under which texts can be obtained, represented, and read.

Its achievement is to make selection visible. Its unresolved challenge is to ensure that visibility, technical rigor, and declared pluralism translate into adequate historical representation rather than merely providing a more transparent account of the archive's existing preferences.

The most revealing question to ask of the library, therefore, is not whether it has finally assembled the correct canon. It is whether a reader can trace each inclusion, understand each omission, inspect the evidence behind each textual representation, and challenge the decisions that made the shelf what it is.

That is a more modest ambition than universal authority—and, potentially, a more useful foundation for scholarship.
